specPoints.text: understand how to determine the percentage by volume of oxygen in air using experiments involving the reactions of metals (e.g. iron) and non-metals (e.g. phosphorus) with air
practical: determine the approximate percentage by volume of oxygen in air using a metal or a non-metal

primer.text: From Composition of Air you already know that oxygen makes up about one-fifth of dry air and that its share can be found by reacting a metal or non-metal with a sealed volume of air. This practical note walks the iron-wool burette experiment from aim to conclusion, including the working that turns water-level readings into the approximate percentage of oxygen.

lessons.title: Aim and method
lessons.opening: This practical determines how much of the air is oxygen, using the oxidation of iron as the measuring reaction. A piece of iron wool sits at the bottom of a burette filled with water, and the tube stands upside down in a trough, held upright by a clamp. Over several days the iron slowly uses up the oxygen inside, and the water level climbs to record exactly how much gas has gone.
keyPoints: First the dead volume from the last graduation to the tap is measured by draining 50.0 mL of water.
Iron filings or a piece of iron wool are placed in the bottom of the closed burette.
The burette is inverted into a trough of water and clamped vertically.
The starting water level is recorded, then read again after 3-4 days.
A little water moistens the inside of the burette before the iron is added.

low.restatement: You trap a measured column of air over water with iron wool inside, then wait days for the iron to rust. The rusting eats the oxygen, and the water rises to take its place, which you read off the scale.
low.analogy: It is like watching a slow leak in a sealed tyre under water: bubbles of lost volume show up as water creeping up the gauge.
low.examPointer: Method questions want the sequence: measure the dead volume, add the iron, invert in water, record both water levels.

medium.restatement: The apparatus fixes a known air volume at the start, and the iron oxidises inside it over several days, converting gaseous oxygen into solid rust. Because the product is solid, the gas volume falls by the oxygen share alone, and the rising water level records that fall against the fixed scale.
medium.analogy: Think of a guarantee: whatever gas disappears, water silently pays back the exact same volume, so the water scale becomes the oxygen counter.
medium.examPointer: Explain why the burette is inverted in water: it seals the air sample and lets the water level double as the volume gauge.

check.stem: Why is the volume between the final mark on the burette scale and the tap measured at the start?

options.text: Because that dead volume still holds air and must count in the starting volume of the sample
options.explanation: The air trapped beyond the last graduation is part of the sealed sample, so leaving it out would distort the percentage.

options.text: Because the tap must be calibrated before any liquid is poured
options.explanation: The tap works regardless; the measured dead volume is air that participates in the experiment.

options.text: Because water will not pass the final mark
options.explanation: Water moves freely past the mark; the volume matters because air occupies it.

options.text: Because the iron wool sits in that region and needs the space measured
options.explanation: The iron wool sits at the bottom of the burette; the dead volume is at the top near the tap.

check.stem: What is the role of the trough of water in which the burette is inverted?

options.text: It seals the air sample and lets the water level show changes in gas volume
options.explanation: Water blocks entry or exit of gas while its rising level inside the burette records the lost volume directly.

options.text: It cools the iron wool so the reaction stays slow
options.explanation: The reaction is slow anyway over days; the water's job is sealing and volume display, not temperature control.

options.text: It dissolves the oxygen out of the air sample
options.explanation: Dissolved oxygen would spoil the measurement; the sealed air is meant to lose its oxygen to the iron, not the water.

options.text: It cleans the iron wool so it reacts cleanly
options.explanation: No cleaning is involved; iron wool is added dry to the closed burette above the water.

check.stem: Why are the water levels read at the start and again only after 3-4 days?

options.text: Because the iron oxidises slowly, so the oxygen is only fully used up after several days
options.explanation: Rusting proceeds gradually; reading too early would leave oxygen unreacted and the result short of the true value.

options.text: Because the water level needs time to settle at the same height everywhere
options.explanation: Levels settle within moments; the wait is for the chemistry, not for the physics of the water.
options.misconception: settling time confused with reaction time

options.text: Because the burette scale only works after four days
options.explanation: The scale can be read at any time; the four days belong to the oxidation of the iron.

options.text: Because the tap must be opened daily to release pressure
options.explanation: The tap stays closed throughout; opening it would break the sealed sample.

check.stem: Which statement links this practical to the composition of air?

options.text: The oxygen share it measures should come out at about one-fifth, matching the approximate 20 percent of oxygen in dry air
options.explanation: The practical is the experimental check on the quoted composition, and its answer is the familiar one-fifth.

options.text: It measures the nitrogen share, which is the larger part of air
options.explanation: Nitrogen never reacts in the burette; only the oxygen is removed and therefore measured.

options.text: It measures the carbon dioxide share, which is rising year by year
options.explanation: Carbon dioxide is a trace gas here and is not what the iron consumes; the measurement targets oxygen.

options.text: It proves air is a compound with a fixed formula
options.explanation: The practical measures a percentage in a mixture; it says nothing about chemical bonding between the gases.

check.stem: A student suggests using a reactant that releases a new gas as it removes the oxygen. Why would that fail?

options.text: Because the new gas would replace the lost oxygen's volume, so the water level would show almost no change
options.explanation: The method depends on the gas volume genuinely shrinking; replacing one gas with another hides the change.

options.text: Because the new gas would dissolve and poison the water
options.explanation: Solubility is beside the point; the failure is a volume-for-volume swap that masks the oxygen loss.
options.misconception: safety issue substituted for design issue

options.text: Because new gases always react with iron a second time
options.explanation: No second reaction is implied; the flaw is purely that the measured volume no longer tracks the oxygen.

options.text: Because gases can never be produced inside a burette
options.explanation: Gas production in a burette is physically possible; it is the measurement logic that fails, not the apparatus.

lessons.title: Results, calculation and conclusion
lessons.opening: The recorded readings are the 3.8 mL between the 50 mL mark and the tap, an initial water level of 2.6 mL and a final water level of 12.7 mL. From these, the starting air volume, the final air volume and the oxygen volume follow in turn. Dividing the oxygen volume by the starting air volume and scaling up gives the percentage of oxygen in the air.
keyPoints: The initial volume of air is (50.0 + 3.8) - 2.6, which equals 51.2 mL.
The final volume of air is 53.8 - 12.7, which equals 41.1 mL.
The volume of oxygen used is 51.2 - 41.1, which equals 10.1 mL.
The percentage of oxygen is 10.1 divided by 51.2, multiplied by 100.
The result, 19.7 percent, agrees with oxygen making up approximately 20 percent of the air.

low.restatement: Work out the air volume at the start and at the end from the water readings, and the difference between them is the oxygen that the iron used. Turn that difference into a percentage of the starting air and you get about one-fifth.
low.analogy: Like timing how much bathwater drained by reading the depth before and after: the difference tells the story in one subtraction.
low.examPointer: Show every line of the working and end with the percentage; the final mark is for the conclusion matching about 20 percent.

medium.restatement: The initial air volume is the full column, 50.0 mL plus the 3.8 mL beyond the scale, less the 2.6 mL of water already inside, giving 51.2 mL. After oxidation the air column is 53.8 - 12.7 = 41.1 mL, so the oxygen used is 10.1 mL, and 10.1 / 51.2 x 100 = 19.7 percent, the approximate oxygen share of air.
medium.analogy: Treat the burette like a fuel gauge: you compare the tank before and after the journey, and the drop tells you exactly how much was burned.
medium.examPointer: Quote the answer to a sensible precision and state the comparison with the expected one-fifth; that final comparison sentence is often a dedicated mark.

check.stem: Why is the initial air volume calculated as (50.0 + 3.8) - 2.6 rather than read as 50.0 mL?

options.text: Because the air fills the whole column, including the 3.8 mL beyond the scale, less the 2.6 mL of water already inside
options.explanation: The starting sample is the air trapped between the water surface and the tap, so both the dead volume and the initial water must be accounted for.

options.text: Because the burette only measures accurately below 50 mL
options.explanation: The scale stops at 50 mL but the air continues to the tap; that extra air is real and must be included.
options.misconception: scale limit treated as sample limit

options.text: Because the 2.6 mL of water adds to the air volume
options.explanation: Water inside the burette takes up space, so it must be subtracted from, not added to, the air column.
options.misconception: correction applied in the wrong direction

options.text: Because the iron wool displaces 3.8 mL of air
options.explanation: The 3.8 mL is the measured space between scale and tap, not the iron wool's volume.

check.stem: The final air volume works out as 41.1 mL. Which line of working produces it?

options.explanation: The whole column of 50.0 plus 3.8 is 53.8 mL, and the risen water now occupies 12.7 mL, leaving 41.1 mL of air.
That drops the 3.8 mL dead volume from the column, undercounting the air present at the end.
options.misconception: dead volume dropped from the working

options.explanation: That mixes the initial net volume with the final water level; the final column starts from the full 53.8 mL.
That is the water's own rise, 10.1 mL, which is the oxygen volume rather than the final air volume.
options.misconception: oxygen volume mislabelled as air volume

check.stem: What does the difference 51.2 - 41.1 = 10.1 mL represent?

options.text: The volume of oxygen that the iron removed from the sealed air sample
options.explanation: Only the oxygen left the gas phase, so the fall in air volume is exactly the oxygen volume.

options.text: The volume of water added to the trough
options.explanation: The trough water is untouched as a quantity; the 10.1 mL is inside the burette readings.
options.misconception: quantity attributed to the wrong vessel

options.text: The volume of nitrogen that reacted with the iron
options.explanation: Nitrogen does not react here; if it had, the result could not be an oxygen percentage.

options.text: The error margin of the experiment
options.explanation: It is the measured oxygen volume itself, the central quantity of the whole practical, not an uncertainty.

check.stem: The calculation gives 10.1 / 51.2 x 100 = 19.7 percent. Why is this stated as approximately 20 percent in the conclusion?

options.text: Because 19.7 percent is the measured value and the accepted composition of air quotes about one-fifth oxygen
options.explanation: The measured figure sits right beside the known approximate share, so the conclusion rounds to 20 percent.

options.text: Because the arithmetic was only rough and could be out by several percent
options.explanation: The arithmetic is exact as far as it goes; the rounding reflects the comparison with the accepted value, not sloppy working.

options.text: Because some nitrogen also reacted and inflated the figure
options.explanation: No nitrogen reacts; the closeness of 19.7 to 20 percent is the experiment succeeding, not an error to excuse.

options.text: Because the burette measures mass rather than volume
options.explanation: The burette is a volume instrument throughout; the percentage is genuinely by volume.

check.stem: Which final sentence best closes this practical write-up?

options.text: The oxygen takes up approximately 20 percent of the air
options.explanation: It states the measured result rounded sensibly and connects it to the accepted composition, which is the role of the conclusion.

options.text: The iron wool dissolved completely during the week
options.explanation: The iron rusts rather than dissolves, and the conclusion should state the oxygen percentage, not the iron's fate.

options.text: The experiment failed because the water rose
options.explanation: The rising water is the experiment working; a failed run would show little or no rise.

options.text: Air contains about 80 percent oxygen by volume
options.explanation: That inverts the composition; 80 percent belongs to nitrogen, and the measurement itself says otherwise.

glossary.definition: A long graduated tube with a tap, used here upside down to hold and measure the trapped air column.
A reaction in which a substance gains oxygen, such as iron turning to rust in this practical.
The volume of air sealed in the burette at the start, worked out as 51.2 mL in this run.
The height of the water surface inside the burette, read off the scale at the start and after several days.
A strand of fine iron fibres that rusts through its whole length, using up the oxygen around it.

workedExample.prompt: A burette with iron wool inside is inverted in a trough of water. The volume between the 50 mL mark and the tap is 3.8 mL, the initial water level is 2.6 mL and the final water level after several days is 12.7 mL. Determine the approximate percentage by volume of oxygen in air.
steps: The oxygen takes up approximately 20% of the air.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The percentage of oxygen in the air is 19.7%.
